description: We are team NebuLa? from METU Development Schools High School in İzmir, Türkiye. We want to think, design and learn.
summary: We built an interactive map that a crew on Mars could use inside their habitat to plan safe Marswalks in search of water ice. Our site is Moreux crater in Protonilus Mensae, next to NASA's proposed Protonilus Mensae human exploration zone, where debris-covered glaciers hold large amounts of buried ice. The map layers three kinds of NASA data (optical, thermal and topographic) with ice, mineral and dune catalogues. It shows a flat, firm camp site, four rover routes with elevation profiles, the last stretch of each route on foot, and safety warnings for steep slopes, dunes and dusty ground. It matters because water ice is the key resource for drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel, and astronaut safety comes first. details:
What it does. Moreux Camp Map is a planning display for the habitat. The crew picks a base layer (optical, day infrared, night thermal or topographic) and an overlay with adjustable opacity, then toggles the science and safety layers. Clicking anywhere on the map gives the position, elevation, slope, night thermal brightness, distance from camp and the safety notes that apply at that point.

Science goal. Find and sample water ice and water-formed minerals. Protonilus Mensae has debris-covered glaciers; radar surveys show that the lobate debris aprons in Deuteronilus and Protonilus Mensae are more than 80% water ice (Petersen et al. 2018). Moreux crater adds glacier-like forms on its walls, glacial meltwater valleys, and clay, silica and hydrous mineral detections on its central peak.

Camp. The camp sits on the flat Moreux crater floor at 41.20° N, 44.40° E, elevation −4,145 m, slope 0.4°. The night thermal layer shows firm ground there (brightness 96/100), and the nearest mapped dune field is 7.8 km away. We placed the camp in Moreux, 72 km west of the edge of NASA's Protonilus Mensae exploration zone, because the zone holds 35 glacier-like forms but none of the mapped mineral detections.

Routes. Four rover routes, each with an elevation and thermal profile and close-up CTX images of every stop:

- South Wall glaciers: 78 km, four glacier fronts.

- West Wall: 128 km, two glacier fronts.

- East Wall valleys: 159 km, one glacier front and two meltwater valleys.

- Central Peak loop: 239 km, silica, clay and hydrous mineral detections, and two glacier-like forms. It goes around the east side of the dune field.

At each stop the rover parks and the astronauts walk the last stretch. The map shows the walking distance, the climb and the steepest slope, and flags walks that are too long or too steep for a Marswalk.

Safety. Routes avoid dune fields, penalise slopes above 15° and block slopes above 25°. The map flags dusty ground (dark in the night thermal layer), places where the central peak may block radio line of sight to camp, and distance rings at 25, 50 and 100 km. It estimates radiation dose for each route from the 0.64 mSv/day surface average measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument; on a solar storm warning the nearest shelter is the camp.

How we built it. We read every layer directly from NASA/JPL Mars Trek data services, cut out the Moreux area, and computed slopes from the MOLA–HRSC elevation model. Routes are least-cost paths across that grid. The map is a single web page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no server) in English and Turkish.

Limits. Slopes come from a 200 m elevation model, so real slopes can be steeper. Thermal brightness is a relative index, not a temperature. The radiation dose is a rough estimate because there is no measurement for Moreux.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, NASA Mars Trek, Netlify, GitHub.

Use of SI. We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help us find NASA data sources, check our layer descriptions against the Mars Trek data, fix errors in our map code, and draft English text for this page and our slides. Our team chose the site and the science goal, reviewed the data, designed the map and checked all text before submitting.
